g.text: Standard MySQL Binlog Replication is a mechanism that allows one MySQL server (the source, formerly called "master") to replicate data changes to one or more replica (formerly "slave") servers using the binary log (binlog).
🧩 How MySQL Binlog Replication Works
Enable binlog on the source
The source server writes all data-changing events (INSERTs, UPDATEs, DELETEs, etc.) to a binary log.
Replica connects and reads binlog
The replica connects to the source using a replication user, requests the binary log, and keeps track of its position (binlog file and offset).
Replica replays events
The replica replays the changes locally using its own SQL thread to stay in sync with the source.
🔁 Components Involved
Component Description
Binary Log (binlog) A log file on the source that records all write operations.
IO Thread (Replica) Reads binlog from the source and writes it to a local relay log.
SQL Thread (Replica) Reads relay log and applies the changes to the replica’s DB.
✅ Use Cases
- High availability (failover setup)
- Read scaling (read replicas)
- Backups (by replaying binlogs)
- Audit/logging
🔐 Key Considerations
- Ensure the source and replicas have the same schema and version when possible.
- Monitor lag via SHOW SLAVE STATUS (MySQL ≤ 5.7) or SHOW REPLICA STATUS (MySQL 8+).
- Secure replication channels with SSL and dedicated replication users.
Single primary, multiple replica setup.
How Uber guarantees 99.99% availability to its downstream services through primary failover
At Uber, we have a single primary-multiple replica setup.
The writes are handled by the primary node, which is replicated to replicas using standard MySQL binlog replication.
The primary failover is an automated process that changes the primary node of a cluster from one host to another.
Since there is a single primary node, keeping it healthy and operational is critical to guarantee high write availability and minimize downtimes.
These primary failover workflows are used as a mitigation action by components,
which continuously monitor the health of the primary node and perform fail-over in cases of any degradation.
Graceful promotions are required during general maintenance activities of the current primary node,
for example, when the host of the existing primary node needs to be repaired.
They involve selecting a new primary candidate and then gracefully transferring the write load from the old primary to the new one.
Graceful failovers assume that the existing primary node is available and healthy.
This applies to async and semi-sync replication setups.
Graceful failover performs these steps:
- Puts the current primary node into read-only mode.
- Shuts down traffic on the current primary node.
- Select a new primary node (primary elect). By default, the workflow picks the primary elect from the same data center.
The replication lag of the replica nodes is also considered, and the node with the most advanced binlog position is given precedence.
- Retrieves the binlog positions in the previous primary and waits for those transactions to apply on the primary elect.
- Enabling writes for the new primary.
In cases where the existing primary node isn’t available (because of a data center zone failure, or network isolation) MySQL performs an emergency fail-over.
It performs the same steps as graceful promotions, with the only exception being that
it won’t rely on the current primary to replicate all the data to the new primary node
because the current primary is assumed to be unreachable.
Types of failovers
graceful
emergency
[Based on the health of the existing primary node]
